title: Failed Window Seals and Flashing: Slow Water Intrusion | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: Why a window keeps staining the wall below it, how failed seals and flashing let water in slowly, and what the damage looks like inside Phoenix area walls.
h1: Failed Window Seals & Flashing as a Slow Water Intrusion Path
intro: You have painted over that same corner twice. The stain under the window sill comes back a little wider each monsoon season, and every time it does you tell yourself it is old, or it is condensation, or it is nothing. Nobody has been able to point at a leak. There is no drip you can catch in a bowl. The roof is fine. And still, something is getting in, on its own schedule, in a way you have not been able to name yet. That gap between knowing something is wrong and being able to explain it is its own kind of tiring, and it is worth saying plainly: the fact that you cannot find the source does not mean you are imagining the problem.

sections.heading: A window leak almost never looks like a leak
sections.body:
Water coming through a window assembly does not usually arrive as a stream. It arrives as a few tablespoons during a wind driven rain, absorbed by framing and paper faced gypsum, then dried partway by desert air before the next storm. That cycle is why the evidence is so confusing. You get a stain, then it fades, then it returns darker. The wall feels dry to your hand because the moisture is behind the drywall, in the sill plate and the sheathing, not on the surface.

There are two separate failure points people tend to blend together. The first is the glazing seal, the sealant or spacer that holds an insulated glass unit together. When that fails you get fog or a haze between the panes, sometimes a mineral film that will not wipe off. That is a window performance problem and it wastes energy, but by itself it rarely wets a wall. The second is the perimeter: the sealant joint where the window frame meets the stucco or siding, and the flashing behind it. That is the one that soaks framing.

sections.eyebrow: Why Phoenix builds fail this way
sections.heading: Stucco, sun, and the specific weak spots around a window
sections.body:
Most homes across the Phoenix metro area use a stucco cladding over a weather resistive barrier, with the window nailed to the sheathing and integrated into that barrier with flashing at the head, jambs and sill. Water is supposed to hit the stucco, drain down the barrier behind it, cross over the top of the window flashing, and exit at a weep screed near the base of the wall. When that path is broken anywhere, water gets pushed into framing instead of out of the wall.

Common break points to look for:

Sealant joints that have gone chalky, cracked, or pulled away from one side of the joint. Arizona sun degrades many sealants faster than the label suggests, and a joint that looks intact from ten feet away is often split when you press it with a fingernail.

The head of the window, where a missing or reverse lapped head flashing sends water behind the barrier rather than over it. This is the most damaging single defect because everything above the window drains onto it.

Sill pan absence. Many older installations have no sill pan at all, so any water that gets past the frame lands directly on the rough sill and wicks into the wall bottom plate.

Stucco cracks radiating diagonally from window corners. Corners concentrate stress, and hairline cracks there act as a direct entry point during wind driven rain.

Caulk applied across the bottom of a window frame, sealing shut the very gap that was supposed to let trapped water drain out. Well meant, and it traps water inside the assembly.

sections.heading: Reading the signs before you open the wall
sections.body:
Start below the window, not at it. Water that enters at the head travels down and shows up at the sill, the wall below, or at the baseboard. Look for a stain with a defined edge and a slightly darker tide line, which indicates repeated wetting and drying rather than one spill.

Other things worth checking, in rough order of how much they tell you:

Paint texture. Wetted drywall paper swells and the paint over it develops a faint orange peel look or small blisters near the bottom of the stain.

Baseboard and flooring. Cupped wood flooring, a swollen MDF baseboard, or tile grout that stays dark in one spot after everything else dries.

Drywall corner beads and nail pops in a vertical line beside the window, which can indicate framing that has been wet and moved.

Smell. A persistent musty note that is stronger with a window closed on a hot afternoon usually means organic growth on a wet substrate inside the cavity.

Outside, check whether the stucco below the window sounds hollow when tapped, and whether the weep screed at the base of the wall is buried by soil, patio concrete, or landscape rock. A buried weep screed traps every bit of water the wall collects.

A moisture meter helps, but understand its limits. A pin meter reads only the surface it touches. If the wet material is the sheathing behind the drywall, a surface reading can come back low while the cavity is soaked. That is why professional assessment usually involves either a pinless meter, an inspection hole in an inconspicuous spot, or thermal imaging read alongside actual moisture readings rather than on its own.

sections.heading: Repairing the water source and repairing the damage are two different jobs
sections.body: This is where a lot of homeowners lose a year. Sealant gets reapplied, the wall gets repainted, and the stain returns, because the entry point was flashing behind the stucco and no amount of surface caulk reaches it. Meanwhile the framing that got wet has stayed wet. A durable fix usually has three parts. First, correcting the drainage path, which can mean cutting back stucco around the opening, installing proper head flashing and a sill pan, and reintegrating the weather barrier so laps shed downward. Second, drying and removing materials that cannot be saved. Wet insulation and saturated paper faced drywall generally come out; framing is often dried in place if it is caught in time. Third, rebuilding what was opened up, which means drywall, texture that matches the rest of the room, trim, paint, and sometimes flooring. That last part is why a lot of homeowners end up dealing with two contractors and a gap in the middle. Gold Water Fire handles both sides of that line, the water damage restoration work and the reconstruction and rebuild that puts the room back. If you are trying to decide whether what you are seeing warrants a look, you can describe it to us at contact us and we will tell you plainly what we would check first.

faqs.q: My window is foggy between the panes. Is that causing the stain on my wall?
faqs.a: Usually not directly. Fog between panes means the insulated glass unit's seal has failed, which affects clarity and efficiency but keeps the moisture inside the glass unit itself. A stain on the wall points instead to the perimeter of the window: the sealant joint, the head flashing, or a missing sill pan. The two failures can happen on the same window at the same time, which is part of why they get confused.

faqs.q: Why does the stain only appear after certain storms?
faqs.a: Wind driven rain is the trigger. Water falling straight down mostly runs off the wall face. Water pushed sideways at the wall by wind gets forced into cracks and open sealant joints that would never leak in calm rain. That is why a window can go months looking fine and then stain within an hour of one particular monsoon cell.

faqs.q: Can I just caulk around the window myself?
faqs.a: You can, and it sometimes helps at the jambs and head. Two cautions. Do not caulk the bottom of the window frame, since that gap is often the designed drainage exit and sealing it traps water inside the assembly. And understand that surface caulk cannot fix flashing that is missing or lapped the wrong direction behind the stucco, so if the stain returns after caulking, the problem is deeper than the surface.

faqs.q: How do I know if the wall behind the drywall is still wet?
faqs.a: You often cannot tell from the surface. Drywall dries faster than the framing and sheathing behind it, so a wall can feel dry while the cavity is not. Signs worth taking seriously are a musty smell that returns, paint that blisters or looks slightly textured near the stain, and a baseboard that has swollen or separated from the wall. Confirming it generally requires a moisture reading taken at the material itself.

cta.heading: If the stain keeps coming back, get it looked at before the framing does
cta.body: Slow window intrusion does its damage quietly, and the longer it cycles the more of the wall has to come out.
